lede: Three prices you do not know: a coffee, a scone and a bowl of soup at the same café. One receipt cannot pin them down, and neither can two. Three can. Pulling three unknown numbers out of three facts is all this topic is.
can: Choose the letter that is cheapest to clear, and clear it from two different pairs
Solve the two-unknown pair that is left, then go back for the third value
Check all three values in all three original equations before you write them down

text: Solving three equations in three unknowns

md:
Three prices you do not know: a coffee, a scone and a bowl of soup at the same café.
One receipt cannot pin them down, and neither can two. Three receipts can.
The method is the one you already use for two equations, run twice.

prompt: One tap to begin. In the picture, equations $(4)$ and $(5)$ have had $z$ taken out of them. How many unknowns are left in those two equations?
explain: Two, which is the whole plan: turn a problem in three unknowns into the two-unknown problem you can already solve.

text: 1 Why taking a letter out works

alt: Equation 1 and equation 3 written one above the other, both labelled true, with an arrow saying add the like terms and the resulting equation 4 underneath, labelled true with z gone.

caption: Adding two true statements gives a third true statement.

md:
An equation stays true when you do the same thing to both sides. Two equations are two true statements, so adding one to the other, term by term, gives a third true statement.
Choose the pair so that one letter's terms are equal and opposite, and that letter vanishes from the new statement. Nothing is lost: the new equation still has to be satisfied by the same three numbers.

title: Why the same letter has to go twice
md:
The two new equations must be about the **same** two unknowns.
Take $z$ out of one pair and $x$ out of another and you finish with one equation in $x$ and $y$ and one in $y$ and $z$, which cannot be solved together.

prompt: You have taken $z$ out of equations $(1)$ and $(2)$. What has to come out of the second pair?
options: $x$, so that every letter gets a turn
whichever letter is easiest in the new pair
explain: Both new equations have to be in the same two unknowns, so the same letter leaves both times. Which pair you use is free; which letter is not.

md:
Write the coefficients in a grid and the easiest letter shows itself: look for a column of small numbers, a $1$, or a pair that are already equal and opposite.
Here the $z$ column reads $1$, $2$ and $-1$. Equations $(1)$ and $(3)$ can simply be added; equations $(1)$ and $(2)$ need $(1)$ doubled first.

prompt: Using the grid, which single step removes $z$ from equations $(1)$ and $(3)$?
explain: The two $z$ terms are already equal and opposite, so adding cancels them with no scaling at all.

md:
Number the equations first: $(1)$ $2x + 3y + z = 13$, $(2)$ $x - y + 2z = 10$, $(3)$ $3x + 2y - z = 7$.
Add $(1)$ and $(3)$: the $z$ terms cancel and $5x + 5y = 20$ is left. Call it $(4)$.
Double $(1)$ and take $(2)$ away: $2z$ meets $2z$, so $z$ goes again and $3x + 7y = 16$ is equation $(5)$.

prompt: Equation $(4)$ is $5x + 5y = 20$. Divide every term by $5$. It becomes $x + y = $ ___
explain: Dividing a whole equation by the same number keeps it true, and smaller numbers make the pair that follows much easier to finish.

title: Simultaneous Equations with Three Unknowns
why: The same plan at a steady pace, with every elimination written out in full.

prompt: Equations $(4)$ and $(5)$ are an ordinary pair. Solving them gives $x = 3$ and $y = 1$. What is still missing?
explain: Taking a letter out was a move, not an answer. Every unknown has to come back before the question is done.

text: 4 Put the values back, then check

md:
Choose the original equation with the friendliest $z$ term and substitute. In $(1)$, $2(3) + 3(1) + z = 13$, so $z = 4$.
Now put all three values into all three originals. Two of them built the answer, so the third is the real test, and it is the cheapest insurance in the paper.

alt: Three boxes, one for each original equation, each showing the three values substituted in and the left-hand side agreeing with the number on the right.

explain: It agrees with the $7$ printed on the right, so the three values satisfy an equation that was never used to find them.

title: What actually goes wrong here
md:
Reports on this question say the method is well known and that the arithmetic is what fails: a sign changed on the letters but not on the number to the right of the equals sign, or a multiplier applied to the left-hand side only.
The same reports add that three values written down with no elimination showing earn nothing at all, even when they are right.
source: CCEA Chief Examiner reports, Summer 2019 Q7, Summer 2024 Q11(iv), Summer 2025 Q12(iii)

prompt: Taking $(2)$ away from twice $(1)$ gives $3x + 7y = 16$. Which of these shows the number on the right being handled wrongly?
explain: Doubling $(1)$ makes the right-hand side $26$, and taking $10$ away leaves $16$. Adding it instead leaves $36$, and the letters look perfectly tidy while the answer is already lost.

md:
Number three equations and read a coefficient grid to choose the letter to clear.
Clear that same letter from two different pairs, scaling an equation first when you have to.
Solve the two-unknown pair that is left, then substitute back for the third value.
Check all three values in all three original equations.
Lay the working out so that every elimination is visible on the page.

prompt: Before the reference panel, one check on the recap. What has to be true of your two new equations?
options: They are in the same two unknowns
They come from the same pair of originals
They have the same right-hand side
answer: They are in the same two unknowns
explain: That is the whole reason the same letter leaves twice. Which pairs you use is free; which letter goes is not.

md: The three equations are printed for you and the part is worth eight marks, with three labelled answer slots. The first mark is for one correct elimination, before any value is known; the last is for the third value coming back by substitution. If you cannot see the plan, number the equations and clear one letter from any pair: that alone is two marks.
